093.subtitle: Six names on one syllable, and the hymn names its own tradition

commentary.meaning: Every name in this verse begins with the same consonant, and four of the six turn on a single word, kula. The hymn does this deliberately from time to time — binds a verse by sound and then lets the sound carry a doctrinal point — and here the point is as direct as it ever becomes. The first two names are unremarkable in themselves: she is skilful, and her form is soft. The third names a particular goddess, Kurukullā, whom the tradition places at the moat of nectar surrounding her island city. Then the verse turns and does not turn back. She is the mistress of the kula; she dwells in the kula pit at the base of the body; and she is attended by those who have given themselves wholly to the Kaula path. That is a progression from an epithet to a lineage: from what she is like, to a name she wears, to the school that claims her, to the place in the body where that school looks for her, to the human beings who practise it. Of the whole thousand names, this is the verse in which the hymn most plainly says which tradition it belongs to.
commentary.history:
Kuśala, the first name, is one of those Sanskrit words whose two senses have drifted far enough apart that English needs two words for them. It means skilful, expert, adroit; it also means well, sound, in good order, and it is the ordinary word in the ordinary greeting — is all well with you? The grammarians offer a folk etymology from kuśa, the sacred grass used in every Vedic rite, on the theory that the skilled man is the one who knows how to cut it; the derivation is unlikely but it shows what kind of skill the word was felt to name, the competence of someone who performs a rite correctly. Komalākārā, which follows, is a plain bahuvrīhi: soft is her form. The two of them are the last easy words before the technical vocabulary starts.

Kurukullā is a goddess with a life outside this hymn, and an unusually wide one. In Buddhist tantric literature she is a well-attested figure, red in colour, associated with the power of enchantment and drawing others to oneself, and depicted with a bow and arrows made of flowers; the great Sanskrit collection of Buddhist visualisation manuals preserves a whole series of sādhanas addressed to her. The flowered bow is worth noticing, because Lalitā carries one too, and the shared iconography is a reminder that these traditions were neighbours who borrowed freely. In the Śrīvidyā setting Kurukullā is placed at the ring of nectar-water that encircles the goddess's city, and a line often repeated in this connection makes her the mother of the kula, paired with Vārāhī as its father — the two figures standing to an initiate as parents stand to a child. Readers should know that the sources for this pairing are ritual handbooks and commentary rather than a single scriptural verse, and that the details vary.

Kula is the pivot of the verse. In ordinary Sanskrit it means a family, a clan, a herd, a lineage. Tantric usage takes that sense of a bounded totality and enlarges it enormously. In the Kaula traditions kula comes to mean the whole embodied, energetic, manifest side of reality — power, the body, the group of yoginīs, the community of initiates — set against akula, the unmanifest Śiva who is not part of any family. A definition much quoted in this literature says that kula is Śakti, akula is Śiva, and Kaula is the joining of the two; the verse itself is variously attributed, but the formula is old and stable. So kuleśvarī, mistress of the kula, is both a modest claim — she rules the lineage — and an immodest one: she is sovereign over the entire manifest order, which is her own body.

Kulakuṇḍālayā localises all of this. Kuṇḍa is a round hollow, and in ritual it is specifically the pit in which the fire is laid; the word behind kuṇḍalinī belongs to the same family of round and coiled things. The kula pit is the hollow at the base of the spine where the coiled power is said to sleep with her mouth over the opening of the central channel, and the yogic literature of this school treats it as a real address rather than an image. To say that her dwelling is there is to say something quite specific about where a practitioner should be looking, and it stands in productive tension with the earlier names of the hymn that place her in the thousand-petalled lotus at the crown.

Kaulamārgatatparasevitā closes the verse with the practitioners. Tatpara means having that as one's highest object, wholly given over; sevitā is a past participle in the passive, so she is the one served, and the grammar keeps her from ever being the one who serves. The Kaula path is the tradition that admits the five substances — including wine, meat and ritual intercourse — into worship, on the argument that what binds an ordinary person liberates the one who is qualified. This has been contested inside Śrīvidyā for as long as the tradition has had commentators. The best-known dispute set the samaya school, which insists on purely internal worship in the upper centres of the body and reads every external element figuratively, against the kaula school, which retains the substances. The hymn declines to settle it. Only three hundred names earlier it has already called her the guardian of the kula's covenant and the yoginī of the kula, and immediately after those it calls her the one abiding within the samaya and devoted to the samaya practice. Commentators of each persuasion take their own set literally and the other set as a figure of speech, and a reader is entitled to notice that the text itself does not choose.
commentary.practice:
The alliteration is the first thing to deal with, because it is both a help and a trap. Six names, all beginning with the same velar stop, and four of them opening with a syllable that sounds nearly identical: ku-ru, ku-le, ku-la, kau-la. Reciters skip a name here more often than almost anywhere else in the hymn, and because the sound continues unbroken the ear does not catch the loss. The reliable defence is to memorise the sequence by its sense rather than by its sound, so that a missing step registers as a missing idea.

The difference between kula and kaula is a single vowel and a whole grammatical operation. Kaula is the vṛddhi derivative of kula: the initial u is strengthened to au, giving the sense "belonging to, deriving from the kula". The same process produces vaiṣṇava from viṣṇu, and it explains a great many names in this hymn. In recitation the au must be given its full length, twice the duration of the short u it derives from, which is exactly what separates kaula-mārga from kula-kuṇḍa two words earlier.

Kuleśvarī hides a join. The elements are kula and īśvarī; a final short a followed by an initial long ī combines into e, which is why the compound comes out as kuleśvarī rather than kulaīśvarī. Sanskrit e is always long, so the middle syllable of this name is a full-length vowel. The śv that follows is a palatal ś released directly into v, with no vowel between. In archanā the name gives kuleśvaryai, the ī contracting to y before the ending, while the other five names in the verse are ā-stems and take the expected -āyai.

Kurukullā has a doubled l, and the doubling is audible: hold the l for a full extra beat, kurukul-lā. Kulakuṇḍālayā contains the retroflex cluster ṇḍ, tongue curled back, immediately followed by the long ā that results from kuṇḍa joining ālaya. The final name is ten syllables and fills more than half its line; break it for practice into kaula-mārga, tat-para, sevitā, and then run it as one word, since it is one word.

The names do not fall into even quarters here as they did in the verse before, so the metre gives less help than usual. Take the caesura after kulakuṇḍālayā and breathe only there.

What the verse asks is more difficult than how to pronounce it. Most people who recite the Lalitā Sahasranāma today have not been initiated into a Kaula lineage, and this verse tells them, in the plainest language the hymn uses, that the goddess they are addressing is served by people who have. There are two dishonest ways to handle that and one honest one. The dishonest ways are to pretend to a status one does not hold, and to explain the verse away, deciding in advance that kula can only mean the body so that nothing is being said about an actual tradition with actual practitioners. The honest way is to recite the names as they stand, acknowledging that the hymn comes out of a specific and still-living lineage and that its last name is about somebody else. Reciting a text well includes knowing whose text it is.

crossReferences.deva: महीं मूलाधारे कमपि मणिपूरे हुतवहं स्थितं स्वाधिष्ठाने हृदि मरुतमाकाशमुपरि । मनोऽपि भ्रूमध्ये सकलमपि भित्त्वा कुलपथं सहस्रारे पद्मे सह रहसि पत्या विहरसे ॥
crossReferences.iast: mahīṃ mūlādhāre kam api maṇipūre hutavahaṃ sthitaṃ svādhiṣṭhāne hṛdi marutam ākāśam upari | mano 'pi bhrūmadhye sakalam api bhittvā kulapathaṃ sahasrāre padme saha rahasi patyā viharase ||
crossReferences.translation: Piercing earth at the root-support, water at the jewelled city, the fire that stands in her own abode, wind at the heart, space above that, and mind at the point between the brows — piercing the whole of the kula path — you take your pleasure with your husband, alone with him, in the thousand-petalled lotus.
crossReferences.relevance: The classic statement of the ascent that kulakuṇḍālayā presupposes, and the reason for reading kula in this verse as a route through the body as well as a lineage of people. The poem calls the whole channel the kulapatha, the kula path, which is within a syllable of the kaulamārga at the end of our verse. Note where the ascent ends: not in the pit where she sleeps, but at the crown.

crossReferences.source: Kulārṇava Tantra, chapter 2 (Śiva addressing the Goddess)
crossReferences.deva: भोगो योगायते साक्षात्पातकं सुकृतायते । मोक्षायते च संसारः कुलधर्मे कुलेश्वरि ॥
crossReferences.iast: bhogo yogāyate sākṣāt pātakaṃ sukṛtāyate | mokṣāyate ca saṃsāraḥ kuladharme kuleśvari ||
crossReferences.translation: In the kula observance, mistress of the kula, enjoyment becomes yoga outright, transgression becomes merit, and the round of birth and death itself becomes liberation.
crossReferences.relevance: The most quoted single verse of the Kaula scriptures and the clearest statement of what the kaulamārga claims for itself. Its vocative is kuleśvari — the same name that stands third in our verse — which is a useful reminder that these names were not coined in isolation but taken from a living ritual vocabulary in which Śiva addresses her by them.

references.title: Auspicious Wisdom: The Texts and Traditions of Śrīvidyā Śākta Tantrism in South India
references.author: Douglas Renfrew Brooks (SUNY Press, 1992)
references.note: The book to read on the kaula–samaya dispute that this verse sits in the middle of. Brooks traces how South Indian Śrīvidyā came to have both a respectable brahminical face and a Kaula inheritance, and why commentators had strong institutional reasons to read the kula names one way rather than the other.

references.title: Kulārṇava Tantra
references.author: text with introduction by Arthur Avalon, readings by M. P. Pandit (Motilal Banarsidass, repeatedly reprinted)
references.note: The principal scripture of the Kaula tradition and, for all its reputation, largely concerned with the qualifications and disciplines of the guru and the disciple. Read the second chapter to see the claims about enjoyment and liberation made in full, and the surrounding chapters to see how heavily they are hedged.

references.title: The Alchemical Body: Siddha Traditions in Medieval India
references.author: David Gordon White (University of Chicago Press, 1996)
references.note: Useful here for what kula meant before it became a philosophical term: clans of yoginīs, lineages, and the fluid substances exchanged in their rites. White's account is not devotional and will not suit every reader, but it is the best history of why this particular word carries what it carries.

references.title: Indian Buddhist Iconography
references.author: Benoytosh Bhattacharyya (Firma K. L. Mukhopadhyay, 2nd ed. 1958)
references.note: For Kurukullā's other life. Bhattacharyya assembled the descriptions from the Sanskrit sādhana collections, and reading his entry for her — red, with a bow of flowers, invoked for enchantment — beside this hymn's Lalitā makes visible how much iconography the Buddhist and Śākta tantras held in common.

references.title: Lalitā-sahasranāma, with Bhāskararāya's commentary Saubhāgyabhāskara
references.author: tr. R. Ananthakrishna Sastry (Theosophical Publishing House, Adyar)
references.note: Bhāskararāya was himself a Kaula, and this verse is where that matters most: his handling of the kula names is expansive where a samaya commentator's would be evasive. Read it against the tradition's other voices rather than as the tradition's single voice.
